newsitem.title: USA: Three ex-defense chiefs to attack chemical pact.
newsitem.headline: Three ex-defense chiefs to attack chemical pact.

text.p: Three former U.S. defence secretaries will testify on Tuesday that an international treaty outlawing chemical weapons is contrary to American security interests and should not be approved by the Senate.

The former members of Republican administrations are due to appear before the Senate Foreign Relations Committee as negotiations continue behind the scenes to free the treaty for consideration by the full Senate this month.
Their appearance is part of an all-out assault on the treaty by conservatives who hope to prevent its appoval by the required two-thirds Senate majority.

As Republican Leader Trent Lott continued to link progress on the treaty with administration concessions on other issues, Democratic Leader Tom Daschle renewed a threat to block Senate business until the treaty has been scheduled for action.

The Foreign Relations Committee, headed by treaty foe Sen. Jesse Helms, a conservative North Carolina Republican, will hear testimony from James Schlesinger, defence secretary under Presidents Richard Nixon and Gerald Ford; Donald Rumsfeld, who served with Ford, and Casper Weinberger, who was President Reagan's defence secretary.

Their views on the treaty are already known. They wrote in a Washington Post article last month: "The CWC would likely have the effect of leaving the United States and its allies more, not less, vulnerable to chemical attack.
"It could well serve to increase, not reduce, the spread of chemical weapons manufacturing capabilities. Thus we would be better off not to be a party to it," they said.

The treaty, signed by 130 countries more than four years ago, bans the development, production, stockpiling, transfer and use of chemical weapons. Critics say it will do nothing to halt illegal activities by so-called "rogue" states.
While the pact comes under attack in public on Tuesday, Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott expects to meet White House National Security Adviser Sandy Berger on what he called "parallel issues."

Lott and Helms have called for an administration commitment on reform of the State Department and of the United Nations and on giving the Senate a voice on changes in other arms accords as a price for movement on the chemical treaty.

Lott told reporters on Monday that more progress was needed on State Department reorganization, some progress was being made on the United Nations and the administration had made concessions on the other arms agreements.
But Lott said further movement was needed to address concerns with an anti-ballistic missile treaty with the former Soviet Union that has long troubled Republicans.
Meanwhile, intense negotiations were under way on the chemical treaty itself to try to forge a plan for its consideration.

Lott told reporters he expected the Senate would consider between five and eight amendments to the resolution for ratification of the treaty and also wanted the Senate to consider a Republican bill that in essence would replace the chemical treaty.
Meanwhile, Democrats are warning that time is getting short. Unless the United States ratifies the pact by April 29 it will lose any voice in its implementation.
Daschle said the Senate had to act in the next two weeks.
"My understanding is we are not much closer today than we have been for several weeks," Daschle said. "Time is running out."
